trackText:
By being so relentlessly obsessed with the idea of merging my entire being into the place, I think I finally felt fulfilled the day we walked the Goldie Bush Track.

The path is unpredictable, sometimes almost imperceptible in the density of the forest. It follows the Mokoroa Stream and played tricks on us, forcing us to cross it more than a dozen times where the banks suddenly became too steep. Of course, setting out on a hike requires a minimum of preparation, so we put on our hiking boots, sturdy, comfortable, all-terrain which, once removed, leave the foot damp, slightly tired and dizzy.

To move deeper into the forest, we had to cross the stream several times, which meant taking off our shoes to avoid soaking them. After the first crossings, we put them back on. By the fourth, we decided to continue barefoot, to go all the way like that, with the sticky sensation of cool, damp earth. Our steps and our walk then adopted a completely different rhythm.

We had printed and pinned a tide chart in the kitchen so we could choose the right moment to explore the cave at Maori Bay. A cave alternately submerged and revealed, whose walls, speckled with marine creatures, seem to breathe in sync with the ocean.

Its natural architecture, the volume, the geometry, the mineral density, sends back an almost monastic reverberation, otherworldly, like an antechamber of the sea.

Certain frequencies ring with unexpected clarity, while the roar of the waves remains backstage, as if held behind a curtain.

This time, the aim was not to collect local sonic objects, but to capture the instrument’s very body: the in-situ reception of melodic phrases emerging directly from our mood in that moment. The exercise unfolded into three variations, each like a different hue cast into the same space.

At the edge of a native forest, early autumn, I hear a few insects scattered all around me, playing a kind of spatialized rhythm. I start dreaming the beginning of a track. There’s a pulse, a number of patterns per minute, quite fast — I think we’re brushing against 130 bpm. The idea was to start from what already existed: the natural tempo given by the insects, who also provided a sort of cymbal texture, and build a piece from there. I imagined something rather dry, without harmonies, purely rhythmic.

Then in Muriwai, more insects joined the orchestra. It became a piece that grew by accretion, step by step, through layers accumulated as I made new discoveries in the native forest. My guiding question was: what music could match such profusion? There’s a community of lunatics out there — a whole city living in the trees, the plants, the rocks.

Palm trees and tree ferns surrounded us; the wooden house we lived in stood in a small clearing. Every morning, dozens of birds flew above our heads, from treetop to treetop. There were rainbow-hued parakeets, collared fantails (piwakawaka), pukekos, grey warblers (riroriro), a nocturnal ruru, and various passing birds. A good portion of the field guide to endemic birds that I had bought upon arriving in New Zealand seemed to be living right there in that garden.

The great soloist of this bird orchestra was the tūī. It would often launch into the same phrase — a kind of wild sequence, so obsessive that I simply had to record it. The tūī is not particularly shy; apparently, it enjoys being listened to. I didn’t have much trouble capturing its sequences before later “cooking” them into sound.

Creating music from a place is perhaps also a way of soliciting it — making it resonate actively, assembling the materials it offers us and giving them vibration. The title Shells was born from an artefact. It began with waking up on a beach covered in empty whelk shells. We gathered dozens of them, once we realized they could function as tiny wind instruments. They respond to a very simple acoustic phenomenon: by making the air inside vibrate, the larger the shell, the lower the pitch.

So I began sorting each shell by note using a tuner, and set aside the ones that produced the clearest tones. A harmonic scale made of six shell-notes emerged fairly quickly. To assemble them, we built the structure of the instrument using a dried palm branch and rope. The shellphone was born from there. And later, the improvised drones became the foundation of Shells.

The glacier takes its name from the German explorer Julius von Haast, who named it in 1865 in reference to an Austrian emperor. Its Māori name is Ka Roimata o Hine Hukatere, which means “the tears of Hine Hukatere.” According to legend, the young Hine Hukatere loved climbing the mountains and eventually persuaded her beloved to accompany her. Less experienced than his fiancée, he was tragically swept away by an avalanche.

Inconsolable, Hine Hukatere wept without end, and her tears filled the valley between the mountains, forming the glacier we know today. But the glacier is retreating — disappearing, like so many glaciers on Earth. Hine Hukatere’s tears are returning to their liquid form, in a cold, desperate torrent rushing toward the ocean. The torrent carries sonic stones and disperses a white noise rich in harmonics.
